newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Samper criticizes captive troops' mothers.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper criticizes captive troops' mothers.

text.p: Colombia's President Ernesto Samper on Thursday accused the mothers of some of the 60 soldiers captured by leftist rebels nearly four months ago of acting as a mouthpiece for a guerrilla group.

Speaking at an official event just outside Bogota, Samper said he was prepared to reopen the so-far fruitless negotiations with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) to win the troops' release. But he said the mothers would have to cooperate with the government and not undermine its efforts.

The women have grown increasingly impatient at the stalemate in the process to free their sons -- most of them raw recruits seized by the FARC when it overran a jungle base in southern Colombia on Aug. 30.

This week, one of the mothers, Hermencia Vargas, accused the government of preparing an ambush for the FARC instead of fully demilitarizing a huge swathe of southern Caqueta province between Dec. 6 and Dec. 16 as it had promised.
"The mothers must help us in the search for a solution and not become the mouthpiece of the FARC," Samper said in a thinly veiled attack on Vargas and other mothers who have echoed her frustration.

Samper ordered a military withdrawal from a 5,400 square mile (14,000 sq km) zone of Caqueta but the guerrilla group refused to hand over the soldiers, saying that the demilitarization was not sufficient.

Some military experts believe most of the soldiers are no longer in Caqueta or neighbouring Putumayo province but are being held in small groups among the more than 60 fronts that the FARC has across the country.

Diego Uribe, a former foreign relations minister and member of Colombia's multi-agency Reconciliation Commission, said on Thursday he had held preliminary talks in Costa Rica with FARC leaders to expedite the process to free the soldiers.

He said that the handover of the troops could be the starting point for wider peace talks aimed at ending more than three decades of rebel uprising. A FARC spokesman, speaking from Mexico City, however, said he knew nothing of the supposed talks between Uribe and the rebel leadership.
